title: Measuring Time to First Successful Tool Call Across Platforms
summary: Measure agent tool setup fairly with clean and configured conditions, event timelines, intervention logs, completion rates, and accepted outputs.
body_markdown:
Time to first successful tool call should mean the time until a developer gets a useful result, not the time until a package installs or an API returns an acknowledgment. For agent infrastructure, the useful result also depends on correct tool selection, valid inputs, authorized access, and an output the application can use.


This article defines a reproducible way to compare setup across tool platforms. It reports a measurement protocol, not measured rankings. No participant study or paid supplier test was performed for this article.


**Method reviewed October 18, 2026.** o11 is the publisher. Example tasks, event names, and study choices below are proposed research artifacts. They should not be cited as observed performance or a promise of setup time.


## Define success before starting the clock


A successful tool call has two conditions: execution completes under the intended account and authority, and the output meets a predeclared acceptance criterion. A request identifier alone passes neither condition for an asynchronous task.


Choose a task with a reviewable artifact. For a public-data lookup, require a correct entity and source URL. For a connected-account read, require the expected test record from the intended account. For image generation, require a stored file with the requested dimensions, followed by a separate quality review if needed.


Keep task difficulty consistent across platforms. If the exact operation is unavailable in one candidate, report that as a capability result rather than substituting an easier task. If a platform offers a different but valid route, document the route and compare the same final acceptance condition.


The[agent-ready API framework](https://o11.ai/blog/agent-ready-api-evaluation) supplies evidence levels for distinguishing a documented operation, a locally checked adapter, and a successful authorized supplier call.


## Separate clean setup and configured use


Run distinct conditions. Clean setup starts without a platform account or configured connection, subject to the prerequisites you explicitly declare. Configured use starts with the platform and intended provider access already established.


These answer different questions. Clean setup measures adoption friction. Configured use measures the path from a new task to a result after adoption. Combining them can make a platform look slow because of a one-time consent step or look fast because the researcher quietly reused prior access.


Also distinguish a developer integration from an existing-client setup. Building an SDK-backed application and adding an MCP server to a supported client involve different work. Compare like paths or report them as separate cohorts.


Official quickstarts help define each product’s intended path. Composio’s quickstart uses sessions and runtime tool discovery; Pipedream’s managed-auth guide describes user connection setup; Nango’s quickstart includes authorization and a first function call. Follow the current route rather than an outdated third-party tutorial.[Composio quickstart](https://docs.composio.dev/docs/quickstart) ,[Pipedream managed auth](https://pipedream.com/docs/connect/managed-auth/quickstart) ,[Nango quickstart](https://nango.dev/docs/getting-started/quickstart) .


## Record the timeline


Event Operational definition


Start Participant receives the task and permitted documentation


Platform ready Account and necessary platform access exist


Supplier access ready Intended provider or funded path is authorized


Client ready Agent can discover or call the selected operation


First request sent First actual execution attempt begins


First completed result Execution reaches a usable terminal response


Accepted output Artifact passes the task rubric


Use one consistent clock source for elapsed intervals within a session. Preserve wall-clock timestamps for audit and cross-system correlation. If different systems supply timestamps, document clock differences rather than subtracting unrelated clocks casually.


Record waiting time and active work separately. An approval queue can create long elapsed time with little engineering effort. An unclear schema can create substantial active debugging with no external wait. The distinction tells a team what adoption will actually require.


## Make an intervention log


For every human intervention, record the stage, reason, duration, and outcome. Useful categories include account setup, credential retrieval, permission selection, configuration correction, schema interpretation, provider failure, and output repair.


Keep categories descriptive. A participant asking where to find a provider key is an onboarding observation, not automatically a vendor defect. A documented prerequisite may be reasonable, but it still affects the user’s path to useful work.


Record assistance. If a researcher gives a hint, mark the time and content of that hint. An assisted completion should not silently count as unaided. If help is part of the intended commercial experience, evaluate it as a separate supported condition.


Do not retain secrets in screen recordings or logs. Use approved test identities and redact credentials before sharing artifacts. The protocol needs evidence of setup steps, not copies of access tokens.


## Use a preregistered study sheet


Before testing, write a short study sheet with the task, platforms, versions, documentation URLs, participant prerequisites, device/environment, allowed assistance, timeout, spending allowance, and acceptance rubric.


Then prepare an empty event ledger with these fields:


```text
session_id, participant_id, platform, condition, task_id
event_name, elapsed_seconds, active_seconds, wait_reason
attempt_id, outcome, assistance_used, artifact_reference
```


This is a template, not a dataset. Fill it only from actual observations. Keep a separate configuration record so the event ledger does not need to carry sensitive account details.


Declare exclusions before the study. For example, an unrelated local network outage may justify repeating a session, but preserve the original record and reason. Do not exclude ordinary setup failures simply because they make a platform’s result less attractive.


## Control learning and experience


A developer who has already integrated three tools understands the task better by the fourth trial. If every participant tests the same platform last, order can bias the result.


Balance or randomize platform order. Record prior experience with each product and with the underlying supplier. Consider separate results for new and experienced participants instead of assuming their setup times should be pooled.


Keep task prompts equivalent. Do not give one candidate exact operation names while asking another to discover them unaided. If discovery is the feature being evaluated, make that explicit and preserve the same available task context.


Use current documentation and record its verification date. Product setup paths change quickly. If a vendor fixes a material issue during the study, report a new condition rather than rewriting the old observation as if the fix existed at the time.


## Handle timeouts and incomplete setups


A session that does not complete within the time limit is still a result. Record the stage reached, reason, assistance, and whether the task was blocked by access, configuration, execution, or output quality.


Do not average successful times while hiding the completion rate. A product with a quick median among a few completions may still create substantial adoption risk if many participants never reach success.


Report counts alongside times: assigned sessions, completions, assisted completions, timeouts, and capability mismatches. For a small sample, show the individual observations or distribution and state that the evidence is limited.


Avoid converting an uncompleted setup into an invented duration. Treat it as incomplete at the declared limit. If you later run an assisted recovery session, preserve that as an additional condition with its own timing.


## Calculate and report the results


Use straightforward definitions:


```text
elapsed setup = accepted-output time - start time
active setup = sum of observed active-work intervals
completion rate = accepted sessions / assigned sessions
intervention rate = sessions needing help / assigned sessions
```


Report medians and ranges for completed sessions, paired with completion counts and limitations. If you estimate confidence intervals, choose and describe an appropriate method before interpreting small differences. A modest sample does not justify universal claims about all developers or tasks.


Break down stages to explain the result. One platform may reduce provider signup while another improves tool discovery. A single headline time hides that useful distinction.


For economic context, keep runtime charges and researcher effort separate. The[workflow cost comparison guide](https://o11.ai/blog/compare-research-workflow-costs) adds accepted-output economics. The[hidden API setup cost guide](https://o11.ai/blog/hidden-api-setup-cost) helps translate intervention categories into practical engineering responsibilities.


## Publish a verifiable conclusion


A defensible conclusion identifies the tested task, environment, participant profile, and observed result. It does not turn one successful setup into a claim that a platform always takes a fixed number of seconds.


Publish the task rubric, empty ledger template, configuration references, redacted observations, and failure categories when you are permitted to share them. Disclose that o11 or another evaluated vendor funded or authored the study.


Use findings to improve the setup path. A repeated account-selection mistake suggests clearer identity presentation. A repeated schema failure suggests a better contract. A long supplier approval wait suggests setting expectations earlier.


The purpose of measuring first success is to understand how quickly a developer can give an agent a genuinely useful capability. A careful timeline makes that claim reviewable and shows exactly which setup work a shared tool platform removes.
